title: The Dishonesty Inside Trump’s New Tariff Plan
gist: Fareed Zakaria argues that after the Supreme Court struck down the 'Liberation Day' tariffs in February 2026, the Trump administration rebuilt near-identical levies of 10-12.5 percent on 60 economies using a spurious forced-labor rationale — plus never-before-used Section 338 of Smoot-Hawley for Canada — requiring federal agencies to certify a known falsehood. He marshals hard data against the policy: manufacturing construction spending down from ~$250bn to ~$175bn annualized, manufacturing employment down ~75,000, and a 50 percent aluminum tariff that Rio Tinto refused to answer with a US smelter.

themes.theme: Legal workaround after the Supreme Court struck the tariffs

insights.claim: In February 2026 the Supreme Court struck down Trump's sweeping 'Liberation Day' levies, ruling the president lacked emergency powers to tax imports from almost every country on earth.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: The judicial ceiling on emergency tariff authority is established — future tariff shocks must run through narrower statutes, which are slower and more litigable.
insights.locator: For those who thought the Supreme Court had ended

insights.claim: After a temporary global tariff expired, the administration imposed tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on 60 economies covering more than 80 countries on claims of unfair trade practices.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: A near-universal 10-12.5 percent import tax floor is now the operating baseline for US cost structures regardless of the court ruling.
insights.locator: First came a temporary global tariff

insights.claim: For Canada specifically, Trump invoked Section 338 of the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 — a provision that had never been used before.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: Reaching for a 96-year-old never-invoked statute signals both determination and litigation risk — Canadian trade exposure carries high headline volatility.
insights.locator: For Canada, Trump reached back to Section 338

insights.claim: The legal rationale for the new sweeping tariffs is alleged failure to keep forced-labor products out of markets, applied to countries ranging from Cambodia and China to Norway, Japan and Australia — a charge so obviously spurious it reveals itself as a pretext to evade the Supreme Court ruling.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: A pretextual legal basis means the tariffs are vulnerable to a second round of litigation — a real, underpriced reversal scenario for import-cost forecasts.
insights.quote: The charge is so obviously spurious and sweeping (Sweden is as bad as Cambodia?) that it gives away the game.
insights.locator: For these new sweeping tariffs, the rationale

insights.claim: The deeper harm is institutional: agencies must publish findings, construct legal arguments and affix the authority of the American state to a manufactured falsehood, which is how institutions are corrupted — first asked to bend the truth, then to attest to the lie, until the lies become routine.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: Degradation of official US findings reduces the informational value of federal agency data and determinations — a slow-burn risk to any model relying on them.
insights.quote: First they are asked to bend the truth, then to attest to the lie. And then the lies become routine, so no one thinks they are unusual.
insights.locator: This is more than ordinary political spin

insights.claim: Walk Free's Global Slavery Index estimates the United States imports $169.6 billion of goods annually at risk of being made with forced labor, by far the highest total among the G20 — undercutting the moral posture of the forced-labor tariff rationale.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: The US is the largest importer of at-risk goods, so a genuine forced-labor enforcement regime would hit US supply chains hardest — an argument the policy cannot survive on its own terms.
insights.locator: Incidentally, Walk Free, the human rights group

themes.theme: Manufacturing data contradicting the reshoring narrative

insights.claim: Spending on U.S. manufacturing construction, which surged under Joe Biden and peaked at roughly $250 billion at an annual rate in September 2024, had fallen to about $175 billion by May 2026 — a 30 percent decline.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: Factory construction spending is the cleanest forward indicator of reshoring; a 30 percent drawdown is bearish for industrial construction, equipment and related capex chains.
insights.locator: The economic case against tariffs is stronger by the day

insights.claim: U.S. manufacturing employment is down roughly 75,000 jobs since Trump returned to office, the opposite of the tariff policy's stated purpose.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: Falling factory payrolls under maximal tariff protection is direct evidence against the protectionist jobs thesis — watch for political pressure to soften tariffs into the midterms.
insights.locator: Manufacturing employment is down roughly 75,000 jobs

insights.claim: Factory output has risen but the gains are concentrated in advanced manufacturing and artificial intelligence, much of it reflecting investments planned before Trump took office and little of it related to tariffs.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: Attribute the industrial-output beat to the AI capex cycle, not trade policy — the durable driver is datacenter and semiconductor buildout, not protection.
insights.locator: Factory output has risen, but the gains are concentrated

themes.theme: Aluminum case study: taxing the downstream to protect the upstream

insights.claim: FALCO, a small Arizona maker of aluminum parts for commercial aircraft, has seen its aluminum costs rise 72 percent and cannot substitute domestic metal because U.S. production meets only about half of U.S. demand and much of that output is not available on the open market.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: Domestic aluminum supply physically cannot backfill imports, so the tariff is a pure cost pass-through — margin pressure across aerospace, auto and packaging supply chains.

insights.claim: In response to tariff costs FALCO froze hiring, postponed expansion, let its workforce shrink by at least 20 percent through attrition, dipped into cash reserves and added a 'tariff surcharge' to customer bills.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: The adaptation sequence — hiring freeze, attrition, cash drawdown, surcharge — is the template for how tariff costs reach consumer prices with a lag.

insights.claim: Trump doubled the tariff on imported aluminum to 50 percent and offered producers a discount for building U.S. smelters, but Rio Tinto — one of the world's largest aluminum producers — immediately declined.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: A major producer publicly refusing a subsidized smelter offer signals US smelting economics remain uncompetitive even at a 50 percent tariff — no supply response is coming.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, even after the so-called Liberation Day fallout

insights.claim: The aluminum tariff achieved a trifecta of failure: higher costs for an American manufacturer, fewer jobs and less investment at that manufacturer, and no new smelter from the foreign producer it was meant to entice.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: A tariff that raises input costs without inducing domestic capacity is pure deadweight — expect eventual exemption carve-outs as downstream lobbying intensifies.
insights.quote: So the tariff has achieved a trifecta: higher costs for an American manufacturer, fewer jobs and less investment there, and no new smelter from the foreign producer it was meant to entice.
insights.locator: Rio Tinto, one of the world’s largest aluminum producers

insights.claim: Aluminum smelting accounts for only a small fraction of American aluminum jobs, with the vast majority in recycling and in the midstream and downstream industries turning metal into aircraft parts, cars, cans, machinery and building materials — so the tariff protects a tiny upstream slice by taxing a far larger industrial base.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: The upstream/downstream employment ratio is the general test for whether any input tariff is net job-destroying — applies equally to steel, copper and chemicals.
insights.locator: Aluminum smelting accounts for only a small fraction

themes.theme: America as the most protectionist advanced economy

insights.claim: After eight decades of leading the world toward open markets, the United States has in barely two years become effectively the most protectionist major advanced economy.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: A structural regime change in global trade leadership — reprice supply-chain location decisions and expect competing blocs to formalize around the US absence.
insights.quote: In barely two years, Trump has transformed it into effectively the most protectionist major advanced economy.
insights.locator: For eight decades, the U.S. led the world

insights.claim: The net result of the tariff program has been higher prices, weaker investment and fewer manufacturing jobs rather than a manufacturing renaissance, alongside a government increasingly willing to make falsehood official policy to defend a failed economic creed.
insights.speaker: Fareed Zakaria
insights.so_what: Tariffs are functioning as a stagflationary input — higher prices with weaker capex — which complicates the Fed's reaction function.
insights.locator: The result has not been a manufacturing renaissance
